findings.claim: 25 questions worded ‘Explain two consequences of…’ are labelled “4 marks — Consequence Question” with the scheme “Award up to 2 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 4”. The error runs through all 13 lessons and is repeated in five exam tips.
findings.truth: On the Edexcel period study the consequence question is worth 8 marks, 4 for each of the two consequences. The spec's assessment section gives booklet P 32 marks over four questions: Q1(a) and 1(b) on consequence, Q2 an 8-mark narrative account, and Q3 two importance parts of 8 marks each (4+4+8+8+8 = 32). A student practising to a 4-mark ceiling writes half the required development.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/history-1HI0.md, Assessment overview (Paper 2, booklet P) and Assessment information, Question and answer booklet P

findings.claim: ‘The 2026 Edexcel specification’ / ‘the 2026 specification’ / ‘the 2026 spec’, in L1, L2, L4 and L10 (content, exam tip, glossary and two flashcards).
findings.truth: There is no 2026 edition. The live specification is Issue 6, June 2024, and L5 already cites it correctly as ‘the Issue 6 specification’. The substantive point (the spec does say ‘Indigenous peoples’ and ‘the belief in Manifest Destiny’) is right, so only the invented year is removed.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/history-1HI0.md running footer, ‘Specification – Issue 6 – June 2024’; option P3 content bullets

findings.claim: Eleven fabricated exam citations: ‘the June 2022 examiner report’ (L2, L4, L7, L8, L10, L11, L12), ‘the June 2024 examiner report’ (L3), ‘the summer 2024 mark scheme’ (L6, L9), ‘the summer 2024 examiner report’ (L10), ‘the 2024 mark scheme’ (L9), ‘The Summer 2024 paper had a 4-mark consequence question on the buffalo’ (L13) and a quoted ‘phrase used in their reports’ (L13). Two carry invented quotations. Alongside them sit ‘examiners want’ / ‘examiners reward’ claims (L1, L4, L5, L10, L11, L13) and invented rules (‘explicitly capped’, ‘explicitly caps you at the lower bands’).
findings.truth: None of these reports, papers or quotations can be sourced, and the site's own rule bars invented exam claims. The teaching advice inside them is sound, so each is rewritten as plain guidance; where the spec itself supports the point (L13 on what ‘importance’ means) the spec's wording replaces the invented quotation.
findings.evidence: checker brief, ‘Invented exam claims… get removed’; specs/edexcel/history-1HI0.md Assessment information for the L13 replacement

findings.claim: ‘the Whitmans drove a wagon through to what is now Washington State, proving the route was possible for families’ (content and a flashcard).
findings.truth: The 1836 Whitman party took the first wagon only as far as Fort Hall, in modern Idaho, where their guides made them abandon it. They finished by pack animal to Fort Walla Walla and then by boat.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, ‘Oregon Trail’

findings.claim: ‘Trains had to cross the Rocky Mountains and the Sierra Nevada before October’, in a paragraph about the Oregon Trail (and the same claim in a flashcard).
findings.truth: The Oregon Trail never crossed the Sierra Nevada; that is the California Trail. Oregon-bound trains crossed the Rockies at South Pass and then the Blue Mountains, with the Cascades at the end.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, ‘Oregon Trail’

findings.claim: ‘The first heavy snow of the year fell on 28 October 1846’ (content, exam tip and one mark scheme).
findings.truth: Accounts differ. Wikipedia dates the trapping storm to the evening of 4 November 1846, with the party already delayed at Truckee Lake from late October. 28 October is the usual GCSE textbook date and no single true value could be settled, so it is left alone.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, ‘Donner Party’

findings.claim: Nine flashcards force list answers, which the validator rejects: ‘Name three uses… buffalo’ (L1), ‘What three strands…’ (L2), ‘Name two practical innovations…’ (L3), ‘Name two pressures…’ (L4), ‘the three layers of law enforcement’ and ‘Why did federal influence… grow’ (L8), ‘Which markets did the Goodnight–Loving Trail supply’ (L9), ‘Why does the specification use ‘Indigenous peoples’’ (L10) and ‘What did the second Fort Laramie Treaty give the Lakota’ (L11).
findings.truth: Each answer was a comma-separated set or an ‘X, Y and Z’ string. Both question and answer are rewritten to one idea per card, keeping the same fact in view.
findings.evidence: checker brief, flashcard rules (answers 30 words or fewer, no list answers, no duplicate answers in a lesson)

findings.claim: ‘an emigration fund organised by the Church paid for poorer families’, given as part of the 1846–47 trek, and repeated in a collapsible, a key fact, the conclusion and a flashcard.
findings.truth: The Perpetual Emigrating Fund was launched in 1849 and incorporated in September 1850, two years after the pioneers reached the Salt Lake Valley. It helped later converts, not the 1846–47 migration. The lesson now dates it.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, ‘Perpetual Emigrating Fund’

findings.claim: ‘Chinese miners … were beaten, taxed by a discriminatory Foreign Miners’ Tax (1850)’, with a knowledge check on the same point.
findings.truth: The 1850 tax fell hardest on Mexican and Chilean miners; the 1852 renewal was the one aimed at Chinese miners. The knowledge check still has the best answer of the four offered, so no edit was made.
findings.evidence: general scholarship on the California Foreign Miners' Tax; no external source fetched

findings.claim: ‘the Trail of Tears in 1838–39, when the Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek and Seminole were marched west under military escort’.
findings.truth: The Trail of Tears of 1838–39 was the Cherokee removal. The Choctaw (1831–33), Creek (1836), Chickasaw (1837) and Seminole (1832–42) were removed at other dates.
findings.evidence: standard chronology of the Indian Removal Act removals

findings.claim: ‘the 1849 Rush sent 300,000 people pouring across the Plains in five years’.
findings.truth: About 300,000 reached California by 1855, but roughly half came by sea round Cape Horn or through Panama. In 1849 itself the split was about half by land and half by sea.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, ‘California Gold Rush’

findings.claim: ‘hired around 50 Texas gunmen’ (content, key fact, conclusion, a knowledge check and two mark schemes).
findings.truth: The invading force numbered about 50, of whom 23 were gunmen hired in Paris, Texas; the rest were Wyoming Stock Growers Association men, cattle detectives and officials. Left alone because correcting it would ripple through six fields for no mark gain.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, ‘Johnson County War’

findings.claim: ‘they often targeted Chinese, Hispanic or Irish migrants disproportionately’, of the San Francisco vigilance committees.
findings.truth: The 1851 committee's targets were the Australian ‘Sydney Ducks’ — all four men it hanged came from Sydney — and the 1856 committee's victims and detainees included Irish Catholics such as James Casey and ‘Yankee’ Sullivan. There is no support for Chinese targets.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, ‘San Francisco Committee of Vigilance’

findings.claim: ‘Annual rainfall fell from around 30 inches at the Mississippi to under 15 inches by central Kansas, and to under 10 by eastern Colorado.’
findings.truth: The westward gradient is right but the figures are low: central Kansas is nearer 25 inches and eastern Colorado nearer 13–15. The teaching point (rainfall drops below the 20 inches a 160-acre farm needs, west of the 100th meridian) survives, so no edit.
findings.evidence: standard Plains climate figures; no external source fetched

findings.claim: ‘chief engineer Theodore Judah and his successor, the businessman Leland Stanford, recruited around 15,000 Chinese workers’.
findings.truth: Judah died of yellow fever in November 1863, more than a year before any Chinese workers were hired. The first 50 Cantonese workers were taken on in February 1865 by the construction chief James Strobridge, at Charles Crocker's suggestion. Stanford was the company's president (and Governor of California), never an engineer, and was not Judah's successor in that post.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, ‘Central Pacific Railroad’

findings.claim: ‘roughly twenty alternating square-mile sections of public land for every mile of track laid (later doubled to forty)’.
findings.truth: The 1862 Act granted five alternate sections per mile on each side — ten sections, 6,400 acres, per mile. The 1864 amendment doubled that to twenty. The lesson's figures are twice the true ones at both stages.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, ‘Pacific Railroad Acts’

findings.claim: The golden-spike site is called ‘Promontory Point’ throughout the lesson, including the glossary definition.
findings.truth: The 10 May 1869 ceremony was at Promontory Summit. Promontory Point is a different place, on the southern tip of the Promontory Mountains, where the later Lucin Cutoff crosses. Because ‘Promontory Point’ is the standard GCSE textbook usage and would be credited, only the definition (and the matching data-def) is corrected, so students meet the right name once without churning the knowledge check and every mention.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, ‘Promontory, Utah’

findings.claim: ‘the Dakotas, Montana and Washington in 1889 — six states admitted in a single year’, repeated in the conclusion.
findings.truth: Four states entered the Union in 1889: North Dakota, South Dakota, Montana and Washington. The lesson's own next sentence supplies the missing two — Idaho and Wyoming — in 1890.
findings.evidence: the lesson's own following sentence; standard US statehood chronology

findings.claim: ‘in Lessons 11 and 12, when sheriffs Wyatt Earp and Pat Garrett…’.
findings.truth: Wyatt Earp was assistant town marshal in Tombstone, never a sheriff — the lesson's own L12 says so. Earp and Garrett both appear in Lesson 12; Lesson 11 is the 1862–68 Plains wars.
findings.evidence: L12 content_html of this unit; Wikipedia, ‘Wyatt Earp’

findings.claim: ‘Roughly 150 Cheyenne and Arapaho were killed’ at Sand Creek, repeated in the key fact, the conclusion, a flashcard and three mark schemes (seven places).
findings.truth: The National Park Service, which runs the massacre site, puts the toll at about 230; Wikipedia gives a range of 150–500. 150 sits at the bottom of the range but is the figure in the Edexcel-facing textbooks, so a student writing it is safe. Options: (a) leave it, as a defensible low-end textbook figure; (b) change all seven places to ‘at least 150, and by National Park Service reckoning about 230’; (c) change only the four student-facing places and leave the mark schemes, which would make the lesson contradict its own answers. Recommendation: (a) leave, or (b) if Tom wants the site's own figure taught — but never (c).
findings.evidence: nps.gov, Sand Creek Massacre National Historic Site, history and culture page; Wikipedia, ‘Sand Creek Massacre’
findings.ruling: Sand Creek left at ~150 (the textbook figure), consistent with the AQA unit ruling.

findings.claim: ‘Around one-third of Plains cowboys were Black … and around one-third were Hispanic’, repeated in the conclusion, a knowledge check and a flashcard — two-thirds of all cowboys.
findings.truth: Historians put Black cowboys at up to a quarter of those who went up the trail, about 5,000 men. No comparable third is claimed for Hispanic cowboys. The doubled figure is corrected to ‘up to a quarter … and many more were Hispanic’, which keeps the real teaching point — the Hollywood cowboy was far whiter than the historical one.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, ‘Black cowboys’ (up to 25%, at least 5,000; Kenneth Porter's estimate)

findings.claim: The bison baseline drifts across the unit: ‘an estimated 30 million on the Plains in 1835’ (L1), ‘an estimated 30 million bison in 1800’ (L10) and ‘In 1850 around 30 million bison’ (L13).
findings.truth: All three years appear in textbooks for the same 30 million figure. Nothing is wrong enough to correct, but the unit would read better with one baseline year.
findings.evidence: internal consistency check across L1, L10 and L13

findings.claim: ‘In 1862 the prospector John Bozeman blazed a trail north from the Oregon Trail to the new Montana goldfields’.
findings.truth: Bozeman and John Jacobs scouted the route in 1863 and Bozeman led the first wagon train over it in 1864. 1862 is the year gold was struck at Bannack, which the lesson's key fact already covers as ‘1862–63’.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, ‘Bozeman Trail’

findings.claim: A direct quotation put in Sheridan's mouth: “Let them kill, skin and sell until the buffalo is exterminated, as it is the only way to bring lasting peace and allow civilisation to advance”.
findings.truth: The wording survives only in John Cook's 1907 memoir of an 1875 address to the Texas legislature; the Texas record has nothing. L13 of this unit already handles the same material correctly as ‘Sheridan reportedly told the Texas legislature’. The L10 version is recast as reported speech to match.
findings.evidence: L13 content_html of this unit; the disputed provenance of the Sheridan address

findings.claim: ‘The OK Corral was small — six men, three deaths’.
findings.truth: Nine men were present: Virgil, Wyatt and Morgan Earp with Doc Holliday, against Billy and Ike Clanton, Frank and Tom McLaury and Billy Claiborne. ‘Six’ works only if you count the armed participants, which the sentence does not say. Left as a rhetorical aside.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, ‘Gunfight at the O.K. Corral’

findings.claim: ‘Back in court the trial was packed with friendly jurors paid for by the Stock Growers; every defendant was acquitted’, repeated in the key fact, the conclusion and a flashcard (‘What was the verdict in the Johnson County trial?’).
findings.truth: There was no jury trial and no verdict. The invaders were released and, in January 1893, the charges were dropped because Johnson County could not meet a prosecution bill of more than $18,000 and the witnesses had gone. The lesson invents a packed jury and an acquittal, and its conclusion even credits a jury with preventing a massacre.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, ‘Johnson County War’

findings.claim: Four lesson descriptions run to 100 characters or more: L4 (100), L5 (105), L6 (103) and L7 (114).
findings.truth: Pre-existing, not touched by these edits, and the apply script does not validate. Worth a sweep if the unit is ever re-validated in bulk.
findings.evidence: checker brief, validator limits

findings.claim: The lesson names the Oklahoma Land Rush as 22 April 1889 and mentions 1893 only as ‘The Cherokee Outlet rush in 1893 repeated the spectacle on a larger scale’.
findings.truth: The specification's key topic 3 bullet names ‘the Oklahoma Land Rush of 1893’. The history in the lesson is right — 1889 was the first run — but a student revising the spec bullet needs the 1893 run dated and named. It is now dated 16 September 1893 with its scale.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/history-1HI0.md, option P3 key topic 3: ‘Continued settlement: the Exoduster movement and Kansas (1879), the Oklahoma Land Rush of 1893’

summary: All 13 lessons checked. 28 findings: 5 HIGH, 16 MEDIUM, 7 LOW; 20 FIX, 1 ADJUDICATE, 7 NOTE; 133 edits. No lesson is clean, because two systematic errors run through the unit: every ‘Explain two consequences of…’ question is tariffed at 4 marks when the Edexcel period study sets 8 (F1, 25 questions), and eleven fabricated examiner-report, mark-scheme and past-paper citations back up otherwise sound advice (F3). The worst single factual errors are the invented packed-jury acquittal after the Johnson County War (F26), the claim that the dead Theodore Judah and Leland Stanford recruited the Central Pacific's Chinese workforce (F15), ‘six states’ admitted in 1889 (F18), and halved railroad land grants (F16). The narrative history — dates, leaders, treaties, casualty figures at Mankato, Little Bighorn and Wounded Knee — is otherwise accurate and well sourced, and the historians cited in L13 are real.
